name: Felix Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the office administrator at a small housing association in an old mill town, eleven staff in a converted bank on Station Road. I book the repair visits, keep the tenancy files in order, type up the board minutes and answer the phone when the front desk is short. I like knowing the tenants by name, like Mrs Okafor who rings every Tuesday about her boiler.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The rota for the repair men wears me out, because one sick day and the whole week has to be rebuilt by hand in the spreadsheet. The pay is low for this kind of job, and my boyfriend Tomas and I split the rent on a one-bed flat with almost nothing left over. What I like is that it's useful work, real people with leaking roofs, not selling anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. I'll read it out. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Everyone at the office has been nervous about computers taking over, and if it's mostly hype then we just get on with it. Online I'd probably share something about how the money should have gone into actual housing instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't fix anything for me. The association is already talking about merging with a bigger one in the city, and if that happens the city office could swallow my job with or without AI. My pay hasn't moved in two years and the rent went up again in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job the way I do it now and not touch any of the new software unless I'm made to. I'd go back to the union branch meetings I stopped going to, because the merger is the real threat. And I'd try to put fifty a month aside, though that's never actually happened yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit relieved about the robots, but tired. The worry I already had doesn't go anywhere just because the AI turned out to be a flop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fifty a month never actually happens. What eats it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bus pass, the phone, and Tomas's car when it breaks, which is about every second month. Last winter the heating bill alone wiped out what I'd saved since summer. I've got about three weeks of money in the bank on a good day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the merger went ahead, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd fight to keep the local office open, with the tenants on our side, because they hate ringing a call centre. If I lost the job, I'd be stuck. There are maybe two admin jobs in this town a year, so losing this one would mean the city, an hour each way on the bus. I don't know how I'd pay for that.

say: I'd tell colleagues the **AI hype** was overblown and we can get on with the job.
I'd post that the money should have gone into **real housing** instead.
think: The **merger** with a bigger city association is a bigger threat than any software.
My **pay** hasn't moved in two years while the rent went up again.
do: Keep the **rota and files** the way I do them now, avoiding new software.
Go back to the **union branch** meetings to push against the merger.
Try to save **fifty a month**, though it hasn't happened yet.
feel: **Relieved** about the robots but tired, because the old worries don't leave.
S0.quote: There are maybe two admin jobs in this town a year, so losing this one would mean the city, an hour each way on the bus.
fieldNote: Felix's worry here is the **merger**, not AI, and it stays sharp even in the mild picture.
He has about **three weeks** of money and few local jobs, so any shake-up is serious.
Union instinct comes first; he speaks of **tenants** as allies, not just customers.

steps.text: Keep booking repairs and filing tenancy papers the usual way
Rejoin the union branch meetings to oppose the merger
Put fifty a month into savings before the winter bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it out. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need unions and rules on how firms use this stuff. Nobody voted for software to do the booking and the minutes. At work I'd tell the others not to volunteer to train it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the tasks they're describing are my whole job. If the association buys a system that books repairs and answers the phone, they don't need a full-time me. Maybe they keep someone part-time, and I'm not sure it's me, because I've never touched these tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get a written promise that nobody is cut because of the new system, before it arrives. I'd cut the takeaway on Fridays and the streaming accounts straight away. If my hours were cut, I'd ask my mum if we could move back to hers for a while, though that would kill me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry and a bit sick. It feels like being told you're the last one who still uses a fax machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've never touched these tools. Would you learn them if it meant keeping the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, if someone sat me down and showed me, but I'd resent every minute of it. I don't trust them with tenants' details, people's benefit letters and health stuff. I'd rather be the person who checks what the machine got wrong, if that job even exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Denise on the front desk, who's fifty-eight and has done it for twenty years. She can't start again at that age, and she's the one tenants actually trust. I'd worry about her before I worry about me.

say: I'd say this is why we need **unions and rules** on how firms use AI.
I'd tell colleagues **not to volunteer** to train the new system.
think: The tasks in the card are **my whole job**: booking, minutes and filing.
If they keep a **part-time** person, it might not be me, since I've never used these tools.
do: Push the union for a **written promise** of no cuts before the system arrives.
Cut **takeaways and streaming** accounts straight away.
Ask my mum about **moving back** if my hours are cut.
feel: **Angry** and a bit sick, like being the last one using a fax machine.
S1.quote: The tasks they're describing are my whole job. If the association buys a system that books repairs and answers the phone, they don't need a full-time me.
fieldNote: Felix sees his **own job** in the card and drops the confident tone he had before.
He would learn the tools only if forced, and frames himself as the **checker** of machine mistakes.
His first worry for others goes to **Denise**, the older front-desk colleague.

steps.text: Get the union to demand a no-cuts promise before the system arrives
Cancel the Friday takeaway and two streaming accounts
Ask his mum about moving back home if hours drop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it out. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments have to step in now, a wage guarantee or something, because people like me can't just reinvent ourselves in two years. I'd be at every protest going. Online I'd be the angry one in the comments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job's gone by 2028, and so is every other office job in this town. The repair men keep going a few more years until the robots come, but the person booking them doesn't. I don't have a plan, and I don't have the money to make one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for whatever union campaign or protest there is, straight away. I'd stop paying into anything that isn't rent and food. If the job went, I'd ask the repair team if they need a labourer, because hands-on work buys me three years, even if my back hates it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panic, if I'm honest. Two years is nothing when you've got three weeks of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hands-on work buys you three years. Would you really go and labour?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to. Marek (the joiner on our repairs team) has said before he'd take on a helper, and it's more than nothing. It just feels like moving to the one place the robots haven't reached yet, and waiting for them to come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomas that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we can't rely on my wage any more and we need to sit down with every bill on the table. He works nights at the warehouse, and that's robots too eventually, so it's not like he's the safe one. I think we'd both just sit there.

say: I'd demand a **wage guarantee** from government, because two years isn't enough to start over.
I'd join **every protest** and be loud online.
think: My **office job** is gone by 2028, along with most office jobs in town.
I have **no plan** and no money to make one.
do: Join the first **union campaign** or protest that starts.
Stop paying for anything except **rent and food**.
Ask the repair team about **labouring work** if the job goes.
feel: **Panic**, because two years is nothing with three weeks of money.
S2.quote: Two years is nothing when you've got three weeks of money.
fieldNote: Felix moves straight to **panic**; the short warning leaves him no room to act.
He spots the **three-year gap** before robots and sees labouring as a stopgap, not a future.
Both earners face automation, since his boyfriend **Tomas** works in a warehouse.

steps.text: Join the union's campaign and the first protest that's called
Write to his local MP demanding a wage guarantee
Cut every bill except rent and food
Ask Marek on the repairs team about labouring as his helper

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it out. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really: we need rules, a proper safety net and the companies paying their share. With five years I'd say we should be planning now, not waiting for it to hit. I'd keep saying it at the union meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a bit better, but I know myself, and I'd probably waste the first two years hoping my job wasn't really going. My job's still gone by 2031, the office side goes first. What changes is that I might get a trade or a course done before then, if I could afford it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd look at the evening plumbing course at the college, because the repair men never seem short of work. I'd ask the union if there's any funding for retraining. And I'd keep working the admin job for as long as it lasts, because I need the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still scared, but less trapped. There's a door, it's just small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd waste the first two years hoping. What would make you start sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing someone like me actually lose their job to it, honestly. If the city office cut their admin team, I'd move that week. Until then I'd keep telling myself it's not real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for the plumbing course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. It's a few hundred pounds a term plus tools, and we don't have that. I'd need a grant or the association to pay, and they won't pay to train me out of a job.

say: I'd call for **rules, a safety net** and companies paying their share.
I'd tell the union to **start planning now**, not wait for it to hit.
think: My **admin job** still goes by 2031, because office work goes first.
Five years might let me finish **a trade course**, if I can afford it.
do: Look at the **evening plumbing course** at the local college in the first year.
Keep the **admin job** as long as it lasts for the income.
feel: Still **scared**, but less trapped, because there's a small door.
S3.quote: I know myself, and I'd probably waste the first two years hoping my job wasn't really going.
fieldNote: Felix admits he would **delay** acting until someone like him actually lost their job.
Plumbing appeals because the repair men are busy and robots come **three years later**.
Money is the block: he can't fund **course fees and tools** without a grant.

steps.text: Enrol on the evening plumbing course if he can find the fees
Ask the union branch about retraining grants
Keep working the admin job for the income meanwhile
Wait to see whether the city office cuts its admin team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it out. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is time to do it properly, so I'd say the government and the association owe us a proper plan. Retraining paid for, not just a website with courses on it. I'd say that at work and anywhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd be thirty-seven when it lands, which is young enough to do a whole trade. I'd still put it off, I know that, but even I'd get moving in ten years. What still scares me is that I've got no money to make the move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the plumbing course part-time over two or three years, paying a bit each term. I'd stay in the admin job while I train. I'd also want Tomas and me to save something, even a small amount, before we think about anything bigger like moving in together properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful. It's like having a slow leak you can actually get a bucket under.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said even you'd get moving. What's different from the five-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can afford a course spread over years, a bit at a time, but I can't afford it all at once. And I'd see the first wave hit other people before it hits me. That's not a nice reason, but it's true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything with politics, with that much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd campaign for the retraining to be free, through the union and in the elections. Ten years is two or three elections. Ten years is enough time to actually change something if enough people shout.

say: I'd say government and the association owe us **paid retraining**.
I'd call for a **proper plan**, not a website of courses.
think: I'd be **thirty-seven** when it lands, young enough for a whole trade.
I'd still delay, but **ten years** is enough even for me.
do: Take the **plumbing course** part-time over two or three years.
Stay in the **admin job** while training.
Save a **small amount** with Tomas before bigger plans.
feel: **Uneasy** but more hopeful, like a slow leak you can get a bucket under.
S4.quote: Ten years is two or three elections. Ten years is enough time to actually change something if enough people shout.
fieldNote: The long warning lets Felix spread **course fees** over years, which is the real difference.
He still expects to lose the admin job, so he stays **anxious** rather than calm.
He sees elections and the union as real **levers** over a decade.

steps.text: Take the plumbing course part-time over three years
Campaign through the union for free retraining at elections
Save a small monthly amount with Tomas
Stay in the housing association admin job while training

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because there's no time and I've got no money. What would help is someone paying people like me a wage while we retrain, and a rule that firms have to warn staff a year before they replace them with software.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who gets the money the machines save. If the association saves my salary, I'd want to know it went into fixing roofs, not into some consultant's fee. The admin job is low paid, but somebody's still got to remember which old tenant's boiler breaks every winter.

headlineQuote: The admin job is low paid, but somebody's still got to remember which old tenant's boiler breaks every winter.
portrait: Felix is **27**, the office administrator at a small housing association in an old mill town, renting with his boyfriend.
He has about **three weeks** of money saved, and admin jobs nearby are rare.
He **never uses AI** tools and distrusts them with tenants' private details.
He leans on **the union** first and wants government to fund retraining.
His mood climbs from anxious to **panicked** at two years, easing as the warning gets longer.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time and no money to change course.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid wage** while retraining for a trade like plumbing.
A rule that firms warn staff **a year ahead** before replacing them with software.
